name: Supporting the Adults Who Support Students
title: Supporting the Adults Who Support Students
answer: Special education relies on a wide team of adults, and the people who work most closely with students often get the least training and carry the heaviest paperwork load. AI can ease that load by drafting short guides, materials, and data summaries, but a person such as a case manager or mentor must review the work and the time saved should return to staff as relief. This matters because a tool that saves time without reducing exhaustion has not fixed the underlying problem.

sections.body: This idea is about directing AI support at the adults in special education rather than only at students. Paraprofessionals, therapists, aides, and teachers all carry parts of a student's program, yet paraprofessionals frequently have the closest contact and the least preparation. AI can produce brief, plain guides on how to prompt a student or respond when a student becomes upset, with the case manager checking each guide before it goes out. New special education teachers also face a steep learning curve, and AI can help them draft materials, organize data, and get ready for meetings so they have more time to learn from experienced colleagues. The problem it solves is the uneven training and heavy workload that strain the adults who make special education work.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a case manager or mentor sits between the AI draft and the people who use it. For paraprofessionals, AI generates short guides on a student's supports, such as prompting during a task or responding to distress, and the case manager reviews each one before sharing. For new special education teachers, AI helps draft materials, organize data, and prepare for meetings, and a mentor then walks through the draft to explain what to change and why, a conversation the text says teaches more than the draft alone. The text does not give separate grade bands, so the practice applies across the special education settings a school serves. Districts can also track how much time AI saves and ask staff how they are using that time.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure, or formal finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its claims come from the working conditions the chapter describes: paraprofessionals often work most closely with students but receive the least training, new special education teachers face a steep learning curve, and burnout is a serious problem in special education with paperwork as a major cause. The text also states plainly that a tool which saves time but leaves staff just as exhausted has not solved the problem. These are practice-based observations rather than results from a named study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on how far AI should go here. A case manager reviews each guide before it is shared with paraprofessionals, so the decision about what a student's supports should say stays with a person. A mentor reviews AI drafts with a new teacher and explains what to change and why, which keeps judgment and professional learning in human hands. Districts are told to track time saved and ask staff how they are using it, and the text insists that saved time should go back to staff as relief rather than to more paperwork. The risk it names is a tool that saves time but leaves staff just as exhausted, which means the measure of success is staff relief, not output alone.
